latency_injection.name: Latency Injection
latency_injection.description: Introduce bounded response or network delay to validate timeout budgets and graceful degradation.

packet_loss.name: Packet Loss
packet_loss.description: Drop a percentage of packets to validate retries, retransmission, and failover.

dns_failure.name: DNS Failure
dns_failure.description: Fail or delay DNS resolution to validate resolver caching and fallback behavior.

tls_expiry.name: TLS Certificate Expiry
tls_expiry.description: Simulate invalid or expired certificates to validate renewal and alerting.

connection_exhaustion.name: Connection Exhaustion
connection_exhaustion.description: Exhaust pools or sockets to validate backpressure and admission control.

dependency_timeout.name: Dependency Timeout
dependency_timeout.description: Force dependency timeouts to validate deadlines, retries, and circuit breakers.

dependency_error.name: Dependency Error
dependency_error.description: Force dependency errors to validate fallback and error handling.

instance_termination.name: Instance Termination
instance_termination.description: Terminate an instance, pod, broker, or worker to validate recovery.

cpu_pressure.name: CPU Pressure
cpu_pressure.description: Consume CPU resources to validate autoscaling and load shedding.

memory_pressure.name: Memory Pressure
memory_pressure.description: Consume memory to validate eviction, OOM handling, and recovery.

disk_pressure.name: Disk Pressure
disk_pressure.description: Fill or slow storage to validate quotas, compaction, and recovery.

zone_outage.name: Availability Zone Outage
zone_outage.description: Remove a failure domain to validate placement and failover.

region_outage.name: Region Outage
region_outage.description: Remove a region to validate disaster recovery.

broker_partition.name: Broker Partition
broker_partition.description: Partition brokers or replicas to validate delivery guarantees.

replica_lag.name: Replica Lag
replica_lag.description: Introduce replication lag to validate read-consistency assumptions.

schema_incompatibility.name: Schema Incompatibility
schema_incompatibility.description: Publish an incompatible schema revision to validate compatibility controls.

credential_revocation.name: Credential Revocation
credential_revocation.description: Revoke a token, secret, or certificate to validate rotation and least privilege.

quota_exceeded.name: Quota Exceeded
quota_exceeded.description: Exhaust rate, service, or account quotas to validate fallback and alerting.

clock_skew.name: Clock Skew
clock_skew.description: Introduce clock drift to validate expiry, ordering, and scheduling assumptions.

data_corruption.name: Data Corruption
data_corruption.description: Introduce controlled fixture corruption to validate detection and recovery.

toolGroups.description: Managed Cloud options for load balancer.

tools.name: AWS ALB
tools.description: AWS Application Load Balancer is a managed Layer 7 load balancer that evaluates listener rules and routes HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, and WebSocket traffic to target groups such as EC2 instances, containers, IP addresses, and Lambda functions.
bestFor: HTTP and HTTPS microservice front doors on AWS
Path-, host-, header-, and query-based routing
ECS and EKS ingress targets
WebSocket and gRPC traffic behind AWS-native health checks
notGoodFor: Raw TCP or UDP traffic
Ultra-low-latency pass-through use cases better suited to NLB
Non-AWS deployments
pros: Host-, path-, header-, query-string-, and method-based routing fits microservice front doors.
Native health checks stop sending traffic to unhealthy targets across Availability Zones.
Integrates directly with ECS, EKS, AWS WAF, ACM certificates, CloudWatch, and access logs.
Supports weighted target-group forwarding for gradual releases and blue-green deployments.
cons: AWS-specific feature set creates cloud lock-in.
Layer 7 processing is the wrong choice for raw TCP, UDP, or extreme low-latency workloads.
LCU-based pricing can be difficult to predict when rule evaluations, connections, or bytes spike.
tools.costEstimate: Region-dependent; in us-east-1 an ALB starts at about $0.0225/hour (~$16/month) plus LCU usage and data processing.
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.
tools.analogy: AWS ALB is like a managed highway interchange — AWS keeps the ramps operating while routing web traffic to the right backend based on the hostname, URL path, and health of each destination.
tools.timsTake: Pick AWS ALB for HTTP and HTTPS routing to EC2, ECS, EKS, or Lambda inside AWS; use NLB for raw TCP, static-IP, or ultra-low-latency needs and place CloudFront or WAF in front when internet-edge protection is required.

tools.name: AWS NLB
tools.description: AWS Network Load Balancer is a managed Layer 4 load balancer for TCP, UDP, and TLS traffic, designed for very high throughput, static IP requirements, and preservation of client source addresses.
bestFor: TCP, UDP, and TLS pass-through on AWS
Static IP and Elastic IP requirements
Very high connection rates
Preserving source IP for backend services
notGoodFor: Content-based HTTP routing
WAF policies that require Layer 7 inspection
Small apps where a simpler ALB is enough
pros: Handles non-HTTP protocols and sudden connection bursts without an application-layer proxy.
Supports static IP addresses and Elastic IP addresses per Availability Zone.
Preserves source IP for TCP and UDP targets, which simplifies audit and allow-listing use cases.
Can terminate TLS or pass encrypted traffic through to backends.
cons: Does not provide content-based HTTP routing such as path or header rules.
Health checks and debugging expose fewer application-level details than an L7 proxy.
Cross-zone traffic and processed-byte charges can increase cost unexpectedly.
tools.costEstimate: Region-dependent; in us-east-1 an NLB starts at about $0.0225/hour (~$16/month) plus NLCU usage and data processing.
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.

tools.name: GCP Cloud LB
tools.description: Google Cloud Load Balancing is a portfolio of global and regional managed load balancers, including anycast-based external Application Load Balancers and passthrough or proxy Network Load Balancers.
bestFor: Global anycast HTTP(S) applications
Cross-region failover
GKE and Cloud Run backends
Hybrid and multi-region services on Google Cloud
notGoodFor: Teams needing one simple local proxy
Architectures outside Google Cloud without hybrid requirements
Workloads where forwarding-rule and egress pricing has not been modelled
pros: Global anycast front ends can expose one IP address while steering users to healthy backends.
Supports Cloud CDN, Cloud Armor, managed certificates, serverless NEGs, GKE, and hybrid backends.
Offers both proxy-based and passthrough products for HTTP, TCP, SSL, and UDP designs.
Autoscaling and health checks are managed by Google rather than by an operations team.
cons: The product matrix is broad enough to confuse teams choosing between global, regional, proxy, and passthrough modes.
Advanced routing and multi-region designs are tightly coupled to Google Cloud primitives.
Logging, forwarding-rule, and data-processing charges require careful cost modeling.
tools.costEstimate: Usage-based: forwarding rules, proxy or data-processing usage, and network egress apply; small deployments commonly begin around tens of dollars per month.
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.

tools.name: Azure Application Gateway
tools.description: Azure Application Gateway is a regional Layer 7 web traffic load balancer with URL-based routing, TLS termination, autoscaling, cookie-based affinity, and an optional integrated Web Application Firewall tier.
bestFor: Azure-hosted Layer 7 applications
URL-based routing
Integrated WAF deployments
TLS termination for regional web applications
notGoodFor: Raw TCP or UDP traffic
Small apps where Azure Front Door or a simple reverse proxy is cheaper
Teams unwilling to manage capacity-unit pricing
pros: Combines HTTP routing and WAF policy enforcement in one Azure-managed component.
Supports path-based routing, host-based routing, redirects, rewrites, and end-to-end TLS.
Integrates with AKS, VM scale sets, Azure Monitor, and Key Vault certificates.
Autoscaling v2 tiers reduce manual capacity planning for normal web traffic.
cons: It is regional rather than a complete global traffic-management solution.
Provisioning and configuration changes can be slower than lightweight self-hosted proxies.
WAF_v2 and autoscaling costs are high for small workloads.
tools.costEstimate: Usage-based gateway-hours and capacity units; production deployments commonly start above $100/month and rise with WAF and traffic.
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.

tools.name: Cloudflare Load Balancing
tools.description: Cloudflare Load Balancing is a DNS- and edge-integrated traffic steering service that distributes requests across origin pools using active health monitoring, failover, geographic steering, and latency-aware policies.
bestFor: Multi-cloud origin failover
Geographic and latency-aware traffic steering
Public sites already using Cloudflare DNS
Active health monitoring across origin pools
notGoodFor: Private east-west balancing
Backends that cannot use Cloudflare's edge path
Teams requiring appliance-level customization
pros: Routes around failed origins without requiring an application deployment.
Works well for multi-cloud and hybrid origins because pools can contain public endpoints from different providers.
Uses Cloudflare edge presence and DNS integration for global traffic steering.
Health monitors, session affinity, and weighted pools cover common active-active and active-passive designs.
cons: It is most valuable when traffic and DNS are already managed through Cloudflare.
DNS steering cannot replace every connection-level behavior of an in-path L4 load balancer.
Advanced monitors and steering policies add paid usage beyond basic CDN plans.
tools.costEstimate: Starts at $5/month for the Load Balancing add-on, with additional charges based on origins, health checks, and traffic features.
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.

tools.name: Oracle Cloud Load Balancer
tools.description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Load Balancer is a managed regional proxy load balancer with flexible bandwidth shapes, HTTP and TCP listeners, backend sets, health checks, TLS termination, and OCI network integration.
bestFor: OCI-hosted HTTP and TCP services
Oracle enterprise workloads
Regional failover inside OCI
Flexible-shape load balancers where bandwidth sizing is explicit
notGoodFor: Teams outside OCI
Global edge routing without another service
Architectures avoiding provider-specific networking
pros: Flexible shapes let teams choose bandwidth ranges rather than fixed appliance sizes.
Native integration with OCI VCNs, certificates, logging, and autoscaling simplifies Oracle-hosted applications.
Supports weighted backends, session persistence, and health-based routing.
A separate OCI Network Load Balancer is available when passthrough L4 behavior is required.
cons: Best fit is OCI-centric infrastructure; cross-cloud adoption is less common.
Regional design requires DNS or traffic management for global active-active applications.
The distinction between proxy Load Balancer and Network Load Balancer must be made early.
tools.costEstimate: Usage-based OCI regional pricing; flexible bandwidth shapes and outbound data transfer determine the monthly total.
tools.addedReason: Added by AI because Oracle Cloud Load Balancer is a relevant real-world load balancer option with notable adoption, interview relevance, or enterprise usage.

tools.name: Alibaba Cloud SLB
tools.description: Alibaba Cloud Server Load Balancer is the umbrella for ALB, NLB, and legacy CLB products, covering application-layer HTTP routing and high-performance network-layer traffic distribution in Alibaba Cloud regions.
bestFor: Alibaba Cloud applications
Regional traffic distribution in China and Asia
Layer 4 and Layer 7 balancing
ACK Kubernetes ingress integrations
notGoodFor: Teams without Alibaba Cloud requirements
Architectures needing one globally portable control plane
Projects that have not modelled region-specific LCUs and bandwidth
pros: Provides native integration with Alibaba ECS, ACK Kubernetes, CloudMonitor, and Web Application Firewall.
ALB supports content-based routing while NLB covers high-throughput TCP, UDP, and TLS use cases.
Strong regional footprint is useful for workloads serving mainland China and Asia-Pacific markets.
Managed health checks and elastic capacity reduce appliance operations.
cons: Product naming and capabilities differ across ALB, NLB, and CLB, so migrations need planning.
Regional and regulatory considerations can complicate global architectures.
Teams outside the Alibaba ecosystem may find fewer internal skills and integrations.
tools.costEstimate: Usage-based and region-dependent; instance, LCU, bandwidth, and data-transfer charges apply.
tools.addedReason: Added by AI because Alibaba Cloud SLB is a relevant real-world load balancer option with notable adoption, interview relevance, or enterprise usage.

toolGroups.description: Self-Hosted options for load balancer.

tools.name: Nginx
tools.description: NGINX is an event-driven HTTP server and reverse proxy commonly used as a self-hosted Layer 7 load balancer for TLS termination, static delivery, caching, and upstream routing.
bestFor: Self-hosted HTTP reverse proxying
TLS termination
Static file delivery beside application proxying
Simple Layer 7 load balancing on VMs or containers
notGoodFor: Dynamic service-mesh control planes
Teams needing managed autoscaling without operating proxy instances
Very complex multi-tenant API management
pros: Efficient event-loop architecture handles large numbers of concurrent HTTP connections with modest memory.
One process can terminate TLS, serve static assets, proxy APIs, and apply straightforward routing rules.
Configuration is well understood by operations teams and supported by a large ecosystem.
Open-source NGINX is easy to package into VMs, containers, and Kubernetes sidecars.
cons: Open-source upstream configuration is file-based; dynamic service discovery and runtime changes need additional tooling or NGINX Plus.
Advanced retries, circuit breaking, and telemetry are less automatic than in Envoy.
Complex rewrite-heavy configurations become difficult to test and maintain.
tools.costEstimate: Free OSS; VM or container infrastructure commonly starts around $5–$50/month per proxy instance. NGINX Plus requires a commercial subscription.
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.
tools.analogy: Nginx is like a traffic cop at a busy intersection — it directs cars (requests) to the right lanes (servers) without getting in the way itself.
tools.timsTake: Pick Nginx when you need a proven reverse proxy, TLS terminator, static-file server, or straightforward HTTP load balancer; choose Envoy for service-mesh behavior and a managed load balancer when your team should not operate the proxy layer.

tools.name: HAProxy
tools.description: HAProxy is a mature open-source Layer 4 and Layer 7 proxy built for high-availability traffic distribution, with ACL-driven routing, detailed health checks, stick tables, runtime APIs, and hot reloads.
bestFor: High-throughput TCP and HTTP balancing
Fine-grained health checks
Connection-heavy services
Teams requiring detailed runtime statistics and predictable proxy behavior
notGoodFor: Static file hosting
Teams wanting automatic Kubernetes discovery without extra controllers
Small projects where configuration expertise is unavailable
pros: Excellent TCP and HTTP performance with precise control over connection handling.
Stick tables support rate limiting, abuse controls, and session-aware routing without an external store.
Runtime API and seamless reload patterns allow operational changes with minimal disruption.
Deep statistics and health-check options are valuable for high-traffic and regulated systems.
cons: Configuration is powerful but dense, especially for teams new to ACLs and frontend/backend sections.
It is not a static content server or full API-management product.
Dynamic cloud-native discovery requires integration work compared with Kubernetes-native proxies.
tools.costEstimate: Free OSS; infrastructure commonly starts around $5–$100+/month per instance. HAProxy Enterprise is commercially licensed.
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.
tools.analogy: HAProxy is like an airport control tower — it watches every runway (backend) and quickly redirects incoming planes (connections) when one becomes overloaded or unavailable.
tools.timsTake: Pick HAProxy when precise L4/L7 routing, health checks, connection handling, and predictable proxy performance matter more than bundled web-server features; use Nginx when static content and simpler web configuration are central.

tools.name: Envoy
tools.description: Envoy Proxy is a cloud-native L4/L7 proxy with dynamic xDS configuration, first-class HTTP/2 and gRPC support, retries, circuit breaking, outlier detection, and rich telemetry; it is widely used as a service-mesh data plane.
bestFor: gRPC-aware proxying
Service-mesh data planes
Dynamic xDS configuration
Advanced retries, circuit breaking, and telemetry
notGoodFor: Simple static websites
Small teams that only need a basic reverse proxy
Environments without control-plane expertise
pros: xDS APIs allow control planes to update clusters, routes, listeners, and secrets dynamically.
Strong gRPC, HTTP/2, and observability support fits microservice and mesh architectures.
Built-in resilience primitives reduce the amount of proxy logic each application must implement.
Extensible filter chains make it suitable for gateways, sidecars, and edge proxies.
cons: Raw Envoy configuration is verbose and normally requires a control plane.
Resource consumption and operational complexity are excessive for a simple two-backend website.
Misconfigured retries or timeouts can amplify overload instead of improving resilience.
tools.costEstimate: Free OSS; proxy infrastructure and control-plane operations commonly add $20–$200+/month per environment before traffic.
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.

tools.name: Traefik
tools.description: Traefik Proxy is a cloud-native reverse proxy that watches providers such as Kubernetes, Docker, Consul Catalog, and file configuration to create routes dynamically, with built-in ACME certificate automation.
bestFor: Docker and Kubernetes service discovery
Automatic certificate management
Dynamic HTTP routing
Small platform teams wanting simpler configuration than Nginx
notGoodFor: Maximum-throughput specialized TCP balancing
Teams requiring deep custom proxy logic
Estates standardized on another ingress controller
pros: Automatic service discovery removes much of the manual upstream configuration required by traditional proxies.
Lets Encrypt integration makes HTTPS setup simple for small and medium deployments.
Kubernetes Ingress, Gateway API, and CRD support cover common platform-team workflows.
Dashboard and middleware concepts make routing behavior approachable.
cons: Benchmark ceilings are usually lower than a carefully tuned NGINX or HAProxy deployment.
Provider labels and annotations can become scattered across application repositories.
Enterprise API governance features require additional products or Traefik Hub.
tools.costEstimate: Free OSS; self-hosted infrastructure commonly starts around $5–$50/month. Traefik Hub and enterprise offerings add paid plans.
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.

tools.name: Caddy
tools.description: Caddy is a Go-based web server and reverse proxy whose default HTTPS automation obtains and renews certificates automatically, making secure small deployments unusually simple.
bestFor: Automatic HTTPS
Small services and internal platforms
Simple reverse proxying
Teams wanting a concise Caddyfile configuration
notGoodFor: Large enterprise estates requiring extensive commercial modules
Complex service-mesh behavior
Teams standardized on Nginx-specific modules
pros: Automatic HTTPS, certificate renewal, and sensible defaults reduce operational mistakes.
Caddyfile syntax is concise for reverse proxying, static files, redirects, and headers.
Native HTTP/3 support and a JSON admin API provide a modern foundation.
Single-binary distribution is convenient for small teams and edge appliances.
cons: Smaller enterprise ecosystem and fewer specialist operators than NGINX or HAProxy.
Not designed as a full service-mesh data plane or API-management suite.
Highly customized traffic policies may require plugins or JSON configuration.
tools.costEstimate: Free OSS; self-hosted infrastructure commonly starts around $5–$50/month per instance.
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.

tools.name: Pingora
tools.description: Pingora is Cloudflare's open-source Rust framework for building programmable HTTP proxies; Cloudflare created it to replace its NGINX-based proxy fleet and has stated that the framework handles internet-scale traffic inside its network.
bestFor: Rust teams building custom proxies
Specialized high-throughput gateway logic
Organizations willing to implement proxy behavior as code
Learning from Cloudflare's proxy framework approach
notGoodFor: Turnkey load balancing
Teams without Rust expertise
Small apps needing configuration rather than framework development
pros: Rust memory safety and an async architecture are attractive for custom high-performance proxies.
Connection reuse and programmable request phases suit teams building specialized edge infrastructure.
Cloudflare production heritage makes the design relevant to extreme-scale proxy engineering.
Framework approach gives more control than configuring a general-purpose reverse proxy.
cons: Pingora is a framework, not a turnkey load balancer with an admin UI and ready-made control plane.
Teams need strong Rust and networking expertise to build and operate a complete proxy product.

cannotConnectToReason.postgresql: Load balancers route HTTP/TCP to compute layers only. Direct LB to DB bypasses authentication, input validation, and connection pooling — a critical security vulnerability.
cannotConnectToReason.redis: Cache is application-layer. Services decide what to cache. A load balancer has no business logic for caching decisions.
cannotConnectToReason.apache_kafka: Kafka is async event streaming. Load balancers are synchronous HTTP/TCP routers. Incompatible architectural layers.
cannotConnectToReason.aws_s3: Object storage is accessed by app services via SDK. LBs route to compute, not storage.

cannotConnectToReason.postgresql: A CDN should fetch from controlled HTTP origins, not connect directly to PostgreSQL. Direct database access would expose internal credentials and bypass application authorization.
cannotConnectToReason.redis: CDN cache and application cache are separate layers. A CDN should not connect directly to Redis unless a vendor-specific edge-compute integration explicitly introduces an application handler.
cannotConnectToReason.mongodb: A CDN should not query MongoDB directly. Dynamic document access must pass through an authenticated origin API.
cannotConnectToReason.elasticsearch: A CDN should not expose Elasticsearch as an origin. Search queries need an application layer for authorization, query shaping, and abuse protection.
cannotConnectToReason.apache_kafka: A CDN is not an event-stream consumer or producer in the normal request path. Use edge compute or an origin service if events must be emitted.
cannotConnectToReason.kubernetes: A CDN may target an ingress endpoint hosted by Kubernetes, but it must not connect to the Kubernetes control plane.
cannotConnectToReason.secrets_manager: Secrets must not be retrieved directly by a generic CDN node. Use tightly scoped edge-compute bindings or an origin service when secret-backed logic is required.

Rate-based rules for abusive clients and bots
AWS-native web ACLs managed through IaC

Applications expecting zero tuning for false positives
Non-AWS traffic paths that never traverse a supported AWS resource

Managed rules can produce false positives and must be rolled out in count mode before blocking.

cannotConnectToReason.postgresql: A WAF evaluates HTTP(S) traffic and must not connect directly to PostgreSQL. Database access belongs behind an authenticated compute layer.
cannotConnectToReason.redis: A WAF is not an application cache client. Direct Redis access would mix edge security enforcement with internal state management.
cannotConnectToReason.mongodb: A WAF must not query MongoDB. It should inspect requests and forward allowed HTTP(S) traffic to an application endpoint.
cannotConnectToReason.elasticsearch: A WAF must not expose or query Elasticsearch directly. Search requests should pass through an API that applies authorization and query limits.
cannotConnectToReason.apache_kafka: A WAF does not publish to or consume from Kafka as part of the request path. Security telemetry should be exported through supported logging integrations.
cannotConnectToReason.kubernetes: A WAF may forward traffic toward an ingress or gateway running on Kubernetes, but it must not connect to the Kubernetes control plane itself.

Private APIs exposed through VPC links

commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

tools.name: F5 NGINX Ingress Controller
tools.description: F5 NGINX Ingress Controller is an actively documented Kubernetes ingress controller implementation for NGINX that load balances WebSocket, gRPC, TCP, UDP, and HTTP workloads and supports content-based routing and TLS termination. It is distinct from the retired community kubernetes/ingress-nginx project.
bestFor: Kubernetes estates standardized on NGINX or NGINX Plus
Ingress routing for HTTP, WebSocket, gRPC, TCP, and UDP services
Teams that require F5-supported NGINX capabilities and migration paths
notGoodFor: Teams that assume it is the same project as community ingress-nginx
Greenfield teams standardizing exclusively on Gateway API implementations
Minimal clusters where another ingress layer is unnecessary
pros: Active F5 documentation clearly separates this controller from the retired community ingress-nginx project.
Supports standard Ingress features such as content-based routing and TLS termination.
Handles WebSocket, gRPC, TCP, and UDP applications.
Provides migration guidance from community Ingress-NGINX Controller.
cons: Name similarity with community ingress-nginx causes frequent architecture and migration confusion.
Annotation-heavy ingress configurations can be difficult to validate and govern.
Teams must evaluate Gateway API options for their long-term Kubernetes networking model.

tools.name: Ingress-NGINX (Community)
tools.description: Ingress-NGINX was the Kubernetes community ingress controller that used NGINX as a reverse proxy and load balancer. The repository was archived on March 24, 2026; existing artifacts remain available, but there are no further releases, bug fixes, or security updates.
bestFor: Understanding existing Kubernetes clusters that still run community ingress-nginx
Planning migrations toward Gateway API implementations or maintained ingress controllers
Auditing legacy annotations, snippets, routing behavior, and security exposure
notGoodFor: New Kubernetes deployments
Multi-tenant production clusters
Any system that requires ongoing upstream security patches
pros: Large historical installed base makes it important for architecture reviews and migration work.
Existing Helm charts and container images remain available for reference.
Its annotations and behavior are widely understood by Kubernetes operators.
Retaining it prevents engineers from confusing an existing legacy dependency with F5 NGINX Ingress Controller.
cons: The repository is archived and read-only.
There are no further releases, bug fixes, or security updates.
The project documentation warns against new deployments and multi-tenant production use.
Migration requires careful analysis because annotations and defaults may not map one-to-one to Gateway API.
tools.costEstimate: No license fee; migration, security-risk, and operational costs apply

lifecycle.reason: Kubernetes SIG Network and the Security Response Committee retired the project after maintenance sustainability issues. The archived project receives no releases, bug fixes, or security updates.
lifecycle.replacement: Evaluate Gateway API implementations or a maintained ingress controller such as F5 NGINX Ingress Controller, Traefik, HAProxy Kubernetes Ingress Controller, Kong, APISIX, Cilium Gateway API, or Istio Gateway based on requirements.
notes: Existing deployments do not automatically stop working.
Artifacts remain available for reference, but new deployments should not use this project.

tools.addedReason: Added separately because the retired Kubernetes community ingress-nginx project must not be confused with F5 NGINX Ingress Controller. It remains important for existing-estate analysis and migration education.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Egress Proxy as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A network component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Serverless Function as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A compute component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

cannotConnectToReason.cicd: CI/CD deploys functions; runtime function code should not call the delivery system as a normal request-path dependency.
cannotConnectToReason.gitops: GitOps controllers reconcile desired state. Runtime functions should not depend on them for application request processing.

cannotConnectToReason.postgresql: Do not place high-frequency WebSocket fan-out directly on PostgreSQL queries. Use a service boundary, cache, or event stream so slow database work does not block connection handling.
cannotConnectToReason.mongodb: Do not query MongoDB synchronously for every pushed frame. Use an application service, cache, or event stream to keep long-lived connection handling predictable.
cannotConnectToReason.elasticsearch: Do not expose Elasticsearch query behavior directly through socket messages. Route searches through a controlled service with authorization and query-cost limits.
cannotConnectToReason.kubernetes: A WebSocket server may run on Kubernetes, but it must not treat the Kubernetes control plane as an application dependency.
cannotConnectToReason.cdn: A CDN or edge proxy may forward WebSocket upgrades, but the socket server should not call the CDN as a downstream business dependency.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Search Service as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A compute component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating GraphQL Server as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A compute component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A compute component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Languages and Runtimes as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A compute component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Commerce Platform as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A compute component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

toolGroups.description: Core and Managed PostgreSQL options for postgresql database.

tools.name: PostgreSQL
tools.description: PostgreSQL is an open-source object-relational database with more than 35 years of active development, strong SQL compliance, MVCC concurrency control, transactions, JSONB, indexing options, extensions, and physical or logical replication.
bestFor: Transactional systems with relational integrity and complex joins
SaaS backends needing JSONB alongside normalized tables
Geospatial workloads using PostGIS
Applications extending SQL with pgvector, TimescaleDB, or custom extensions
notGoodFor: Write scaling far beyond a single primary without sharding strategy
Always-on global multi-writer requirements
Teams without capacity to monitor vacuum, indexes, WAL, and backups
pros: Reliable ACID transactions and rich SQL handle complex business data well.
Extension ecosystem adds capabilities such as PostGIS, pgvector, TimescaleDB, and custom data types.
MVCC provides strong concurrency without readers blocking ordinary writers.
Large community, mature tooling, and broad managed-service support reduce adoption risk.
cons: Write-heavy workloads require vacuum, bloat, checkpoint, WAL, and index tuning expertise.
Native single-primary scaling often needs replicas, partitioning, sharding extensions, or a distributed derivative.
Connection-per-process designs need pooling for serverless or highly concurrent applications.
tools.costEstimate: Free OSS; small self-hosted instances start around $10–$50/month, while HA production clusters commonly cost $100–$1,000+/month
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.
tools.analogy: PostgreSQL is like a well-run library with strict catalog rules — information is organized, relationships are enforced, and complex questions can be answered reliably.
tools.timsTake: Start with PostgreSQL for most transactional business systems that need correctness, joins, reporting, and mature tooling; move to a specialized store only when a measured workload proves that relational design is the wrong fit.

bestFor: AWS SaaS backends requiring managed PostgreSQL-compatible HA
Read-heavy systems using Aurora replicas and reader endpoints
Applications using Aurora Serverless for variable demand
Teams integrating PostgreSQL workloads with AWS backups, IAM, and VPC controls
notGoodFor: Extensions or behaviors not supported by Aurora compatibility
Cloud-neutral database strategy
Tiny cost-sensitive workloads where standard RDS or self-hosting is cheaper
pros: Managed storage replication and automated backups reduce database operations.
Read replicas and reader endpoints simplify scale-out reads.
Tight AWS integration covers IAM authentication, RDS Proxy, CloudWatch, KMS, and cross-region patterns.
Aurora Serverless variants help workloads with variable capacity requirements.
cons: PostgreSQL compatibility is high but not identical; extensions and version timing must be checked.
Aurora-specific architecture and features increase AWS lock-in.
Costs can exceed standard RDS PostgreSQL for steady modest workloads.
tools.costEstimate: Usage-based AWS pricing for instances or ACUs, storage, I/O, and backups; production clusters commonly start around $100+/month
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.

bestFor: Conventional PostgreSQL applications hosted on GCP
Teams needing automated backups, patching, replicas, and HA without a specialized database
Cloud Run and GKE applications using private IP connectivity
Moderate-scale OLTP workloads
notGoodFor: Extreme write throughput requiring distributed SQL
Applications requiring every PostgreSQL extension
Teams needing cross-cloud control-plane portability
pros: Straightforward managed PostgreSQL for applications that do not need a specialized distributed database.
Automated backups, maintenance, replicas, and HA reduce routine operations.
Private IP, IAM database authentication options, and Cloud SQL connectors fit GCP applications.
Familiar PostgreSQL clients and extensions simplify migration.
cons: Vertical and instance-oriented scaling has limits for extreme write throughput.
Cloud SQL maintenance and failover behavior must be tested against application retry logic.
GCP-specific networking and operational integration reduce portability.
tools.costEstimate: Usage-based instance, storage, backup, and network pricing; small instances start around $10–$30/month before HA
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.

tools.name: Azure Database for PostgreSQL
tools.description: Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server is Microsoft's managed PostgreSQL offering with zone-redundant high availability options, backups, maintenance controls, private networking, and Azure monitoring integrations.
bestFor: Azure-hosted PostgreSQL applications using flexible server
Microsoft estates requiring private networking, Entra integration, backups, and HA
Moderate-scale OLTP backends for AKS and App Service
Teams wanting managed patching and maintenance controls

Extensions outside Azure's supported list
Extreme horizontal write scaling

Azure-native identity, networking, monitoring, and backup integration suit Microsoft estates.

Zone-redundant HA improves resilience without self-managing replicas.
cons: Extension support and PostgreSQL version availability must be checked against self-hosted expectations.
Azure networking and HA configuration add platform-specific complexity.
Not designed to transparently shard a write-heavy database across many nodes.

tools.name: Neon
tools.description: Neon is a serverless PostgreSQL platform that separates compute from storage, supports autoscaling and scale-to-zero, and can create copy-on-write database branches for development and preview environments.
bestFor: Serverless PostgreSQL for preview environments and branch-per-feature workflows
Applications with variable traffic benefiting from compute-storage separation
Developer platforms needing instant database branching
Teams deploying PostgreSQL-backed serverless APIs
notGoodFor: Latency-sensitive workloads that cannot tolerate cold starts
Applications requiring unsupported extensions or self-managed superuser access
Large steady workloads where reserved infrastructure may be cheaper
pros: Database branching is useful for preview deployments, testing, and isolated developer workflows.
Separation of compute and storage enables rapid provisioning and elastic capacity.
PostgreSQL wire compatibility works with existing drivers and many tools.
Scale-to-zero can reduce cost for intermittent development or low-traffic workloads.
cons: Cold starts and remote storage behavior need latency testing for production workloads.
Not every PostgreSQL extension or low-level administrative operation is available.
Serverless economics should be compared with provisioned databases for steady traffic.
tools.costEstimate: Free tier available; paid plans scale with compute hours, storage, branches, and data transfer

tools.name: Supabase
tools.description: Supabase is a backend platform centered on managed PostgreSQL, adding authentication, storage, realtime change delivery, edge functions, and auto-generated APIs for application development.
bestFor: PostgreSQL-backed applications needing auth, storage, realtime, and generated APIs
Startups shipping CRUD products quickly
Teams wanting managed pgvector and database extensions
Mobile and web applications using row-level security
notGoodFor: Applications requiring deep database infrastructure control
Teams that only need bare PostgreSQL and want to minimize platform coupling
Heavy sustained workloads without careful capacity and egress modeling
pros: Uses PostgreSQL rather than a proprietary document model, preserving SQL and extension access.
Integrated auth, storage, realtime, and APIs accelerate product prototypes and smaller teams.
Open-source components make the architecture more inspectable than many backend-as-a-service products.
Row Level Security can enforce data access close to the database.
cons: Convenient direct API access demands careful Row Level Security design.
Platform-specific services add coupling beyond plain PostgreSQL.
Large production workloads still require database indexing, pooling, observability, and cost planning.

tools.name: CockroachDB
tools.description: CockroachDB is a distributed SQL database inspired by PostgreSQL semantics, designed for horizontal scaling, serializable transactions, and survivability across nodes, zones, and regions.
bestFor: Globally distributed SQL applications requiring serializable transactions
Multi-region SaaS systems that need survivability across zones or regions
PostgreSQL-wire-compatible applications accepting compatibility differences
Systems prioritizing horizontal scale and automated replication
notGoodFor: Applications depending on unsupported PostgreSQL extensions
Simple single-region workloads where PostgreSQL is cheaper and easier
Latency-sensitive transactions spanning distant regions without locality design
pros: Automatic data distribution and replication simplify multi-node resilience.
Serializable transactions preserve a familiar relational programming model.
PostgreSQL wire compatibility supports many existing drivers and ORMs.
Strong fit for globally distributed applications that need relational consistency.
cons: PostgreSQL compatibility is partial rather than exact; SQL, extension, and ORM behavior need validation.
Cross-region consensus adds write latency.
Schema design, hot ranges, transaction contention, and cost still require distributed-systems expertise.
tools.costEstimate: Free self-hosted core and managed tiers; cloud pricing scales with compute, storage, and request units
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.

tools.name: YugabyteDB
tools.description: YugabyteDB is a distributed SQL database with a PostgreSQL-compatible YSQL API, a distributed storage layer, replication, and scale-out deployment across zones and regions.
bestFor: Distributed SQL systems requiring PostgreSQL-compatible APIs
Multi-region transactional applications with tunable replication
Teams needing horizontal scale with familiar SQL
Hybrid or self-hosted distributed database deployments
notGoodFor: Small applications where a distributed database adds needless complexity
Applications requiring complete PostgreSQL extension compatibility
Teams without distributed-systems operational expertise
pros: YSQL exposes familiar PostgreSQL-style SQL and drivers for distributed applications.
Shard and replica placement support resilient multi-zone and geo-distributed designs.
Open-source core and managed options give teams deployment flexibility.
Useful when horizontal scaling is required without abandoning relational models.
cons: PostgreSQL extension and behavior compatibility is not complete.
Distributed query plans and consensus replication add operational complexity.
Single-region standard CRUD applications may be simpler and cheaper on ordinary PostgreSQL.
tools.costEstimate: Free OSS core; managed and enterprise pricing scale with vCPU, storage, and support

tools.name: TimescaleDB
tools.description: TimescaleDB is a PostgreSQL extension and platform for time-series workloads, adding hypertables, compression, continuous aggregates, retention policies, and time-oriented query optimizations while retaining SQL.
bestFor: Time-series data modeled with PostgreSQL SQL and extensions
IoT, telemetry, finance, and observability workloads using hypertables
Teams wanting relational joins alongside time-series queries
Existing PostgreSQL applications adding retention and compression policies
notGoodFor: Massive metrics ingestion better served by purpose-built observability stores
Teams requiring a fully independent non-PostgreSQL engine
Workloads where extension availability is restricted by the managed provider
pros: Keeps PostgreSQL SQL, joins, transactions, and ecosystem for time-series applications.
Hypertables and compression reduce manual partition-management work.
Continuous aggregates accelerate common rollups and dashboard queries.
Good fit when relational metadata and time-series measurements must coexist.
cons: Not a universal replacement for specialized telemetry systems at every scale.
Extension-specific features reduce portability to plain PostgreSQL.
Compression, chunk sizing, and retention settings require workload-aware tuning.
tools.costEstimate: Free OSS extension; Timescale Cloud plans scale with compute, storage, and services

cannotConnectToReason.client_browser: Browsers must not connect directly to MongoDB. Direct database credentials in client code bypass application authorization, validation, rate limits, and network segmentation.
cannotConnectToReason.cdn: A CDN serves cached or edge-generated content and must not query MongoDB directly. Route dynamic data access through an authenticated application API.
cannotConnectToReason.waf: A WAF inspects HTTP(S) requests at the edge; it is not a database client and must not query MongoDB.
cannotConnectToReason.load_balancer: A load balancer forwards traffic to compute endpoints. Sending database traffic from the balancing layer bypasses application logic and connection-management controls.
cannotConnectToReason.api_gateway: An API gateway should route requests to an application or serverless handler, not expose MongoDB as a direct backend. The compute layer must enforce domain authorization and input validation.

tools.name: Redis
tools.description: Redis is an in-memory data-structure server used for caching, sessions, counters, queues, streams, pub/sub, rate limiting, and low-latency state; Redis Open Source supports replication, RDB and AOF persistence, and sharding through Redis Cluster.
bestFor: Sub-millisecond cache reads for frequently accessed application data
Session stores and rate-limit counters with TTLs
Leaderboards, queues, and ephemeral coordination using Redis data structures
Streams and pub/sub for lightweight event distribution
notGoodFor: Durable system-of-record storage without carefully designed persistence and recovery
Datasets materially larger than affordable RAM
Strong cross-key transactional workflows comparable to relational databases
pros: Rich atomic data types solve common application problems without custom locking logic.
Sub-millisecond in-memory operations make it effective for hot-path reads, counters, and ephemeral coordination.
Streams, pub/sub, sorted sets, hashes, and Lua or Functions support more than simple key-value caching.
Large client ecosystem and managed-service availability make adoption straightforward.
cons: Memory cost is high when large datasets or oversized values are stored carelessly.
Cache invalidation, eviction policy, hot keys, and failover behavior need explicit design.
Redis Cluster trades simplicity for sharding constraints and cross-slot limitations.
tools.costEstimate: Free OSS; managed or self-hosted production nodes commonly start around $15–$100+/month and scale with RAM and replicas
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.
tools.analogy: Redis is like a whiteboard beside your desk — the facts you need repeatedly are available immediately instead of being fetched from the filing cabinet every time. Treat the whiteboard as disposable unless you deliberately configure durability.
tools.timsTake: Pick Redis for hot cache entries, sessions, counters, rate limits, and short-lived coordination state; do not make it your primary system of record unless you have explicitly designed for persistence, memory cost, and failover.

cannotConnectToReason.client_browser: Redis must never be internet-exposed. No built-in auth by default. Always access through application servers.
cannotConnectToReason.load_balancer: Redis uses its own binary protocol. LBs route HTTP/TCP to compute. Redis is accessed via Redis client libraries in your app code.
cannotConnectToReason.cdn: CDN caches HTTP responses at edge. Redis caches application data server-side. Different caching purposes at different layers.

realWorldUsage.usage: Precomputed home timelines as sorted sets. Sub-ms feed loads at 300M+ users.
Rate limiting via INCR+TTL and session storage.
Driver locations via GEO commands. Nearest driver in O(N+log(M)).

tools.name: Elasticsearch
tools.description: Elasticsearch is Elastic's distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene, storing structured, unstructured, and vector data in indices split into shards and replicas for near-real-time retrieval, aggregations, observability, and security analytics.
bestFor: Full-text product and content search with relevance scoring
Log and event exploration with near-real-time indexing
Faceted search and aggregations for catalogs
Vector and hybrid retrieval where Elastic licensing fits
notGoodFor: Transactional systems of record
Clusters without shard, mapping, and lifecycle discipline
Tiny search workloads where a simpler embedded or managed search service is cheaper
pros: Excellent full-text search, relevance scoring, aggregations, and faceting for application search.
Horizontal sharding and replicas support large read-heavy and analytics workloads.
Vector and hybrid retrieval capabilities support modern RAG and semantic-search patterns.
Elastic Stack ecosystem provides ingestion, dashboards, alerting, and operational tooling.
cons: Mapping mistakes, shard over-allocation, and uncontrolled cardinality create expensive clusters.
Near-real-time search is not a replacement for a transactional system of record.
License model and feature packaging need review for self-hosted commercial use.
tools.costEstimate: Free source-available distribution; self-hosted production clusters commonly start around $100–$500+/month and grow with memory, replicas, storage, and support
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.
tools.analogy: Elasticsearch is like the index at the back of a huge encyclopedia — it helps you find relevant pages quickly without scanning every page from the beginning.
tools.timsTake: Pick Elasticsearch for serious full-text search, relevance ranking, faceting, and log exploration; keep a separate source-of-truth database because search indexes are optimized for retrieval, not authoritative transactional storage.

tools.name: OpenSearch
tools.description: OpenSearch is an Apache 2.0-licensed community-driven search and analytics suite forked from Elasticsearch 7.10.2, with Lucene-based indexing, SQL and query DSL support, dashboards, vector search, and observability or security plugins.
bestFor: Apache 2.0-licensed search and analytics clusters
Log analytics and observability search
Application search using Lucene-style indexing and aggregations
Teams avoiding Elastic's source-available licensing model
notGoodFor: Transactional primary databases
Teams expecting exact Elasticsearch feature parity across versions
Small workloads where cluster operations outweigh benefits
pros: Permissive open-source license appeals to teams avoiding source-available licensing changes.
Familiar Elasticsearch-style APIs and concepts simplify many migrations.
Plugin ecosystem covers security, dashboards, alerting, and vector workloads.
Can be self-hosted or consumed through managed services.
cons: Elasticsearch and OpenSearch have diverged, so compatibility assumptions need testing.
Cluster sizing, shards, mappings, JVM tuning, and upgrades remain operationally demanding.
Some Elastic ecosystem tools and features do not transfer directly.
tools.costEstimate: Free OSS; self-hosted production clusters commonly start around $100–$500+/month
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.

Vector search workloads staying inside AWS

Applications requiring arbitrary plugins or host-level control

pros: Managed domains and serverless collections reduce cluster infrastructure operations.

cannotConnectToReason.client_browser: Browsers must not query Elasticsearch directly. An API must enforce authorization, query limits, and protection against expensive searches.
cannotConnectToReason.cdn: A CDN should cache application responses, not expose Elasticsearch as an origin. Route search requests through a controlled API.
cannotConnectToReason.waf: A WAF inspects HTTP(S) requests but should not query Elasticsearch directly. Export WAF logs through supported pipelines instead.
cannotConnectToReason.load_balancer: A load balancer can front an application search API, but should not route public traffic directly to Elasticsearch nodes.
cannotConnectToReason.api_gateway: An API gateway should call a search service or application handler rather than exposing Elasticsearch query DSL directly to external clients.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Document Database as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A data component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

toolGroups.description: Document Store options for document database.

tools.name: MongoDB
tools.description: MongoDB is a deployable tool used for document database responsibilities, especially durable storage, retrieval, and data lifecycle management.
bestFor: Document Database workloads in production
Teams prioritizing durable storage, retrieval, and data lifecycle management
Architectures that need an explicit document database component
notGoodFor: stateless request routing where durable persistence is unnecessary
Teams without ownership, monitoring, and lifecycle planning
pros: Addresses a clear document database responsibility
Fits common production architectures
Supports repeatable operational configuration
Has an active ecosystem, documented adoption, or an established enterprise role
cons: Introduces another operational dependency
Requires security, capacity, and failure-mode planning
Pricing or maintenance effort increases with scale
tools.costEstimate: Free OSS; infrastructure and operational costs apply
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.
tools.analogy: MongoDB is like a cabinet of flexible JSON folders — each folder can carry the fields it needs without forcing every record into the same rigid form.
tools.timsTake: Pick MongoDB when your application naturally reads and writes document-shaped aggregates with evolving fields; choose PostgreSQL when relationships, constraints, multi-row transactions, and analytical joins dominate the design.

commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A data component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A data component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

toolGroups.description: Kafka Platform options for apache kafka.

tools.name: Apache Kafka
tools.description: Apache Kafka is an open-source distributed event-streaming platform in which producers append records to partitioned, replicated topics and consumers process those ordered logs independently using offsets and consumer groups.
bestFor: Event sourcing and replayable domain-event logs
CDC pipelines carrying database changes into downstream systems
High-throughput asynchronous integration with partition-local ordering
Stream processing with Kafka Streams, Flink, or Spark
notGoodFor: Simple low-volume work queues where RabbitMQ or SQS is easier
Global ordering across many partitions
Teams unable to operate brokers, storage, rebalances, and schema discipline
pros: Durable append-only log supports event sourcing, CDC, replay, stream processing, and asynchronous integration.
Partitioning scales throughput while preserving order within each partition.
Independent consumer groups let many downstream systems read the same event history at their own pace.
Mature ecosystem includes Kafka Connect, Kafka Streams, schema registries, and managed services.
cons: Partition-key mistakes create hot partitions and ordering surprises.
Cluster operations, broker sizing, storage, replication, rebalances, and upgrades require expertise.
Kafka is not a simple task queue: consumer semantics and retention-based storage need deliberate design.
tools.costEstimate: Free OSS; production clusters commonly require at least 3 brokers and often cost $150–$1,000+/month before data transfer
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.
tools.analogy: Kafka is like a durable conveyor belt with a logbook — producers place events on the belt, and different teams can inspect the same history at their own speed or replay it later.
tools.timsTake: Pick Kafka when you need durable high-throughput event streams, replay, partitions, and multiple independent consumers; use SQS, RabbitMQ, or NATS for simpler task delivery and request-decoupling problems.

modalIcon.name: workflow
modalIcon.usageNote: Generic open-source UI icon. Preserve the Lucide license notice in the application distribution.

tools.name: AWS MSK
tools.description: Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka is AWS's managed Kafka service for provisioning brokers, storage, patching workflows, monitoring, security integration, and serverless or provisioned capacity models.
bestFor: AWS-native Kafka workloads in private VPCs
CDC and event-streaming pipelines integrated with AWS services
Teams needing managed brokers or MSK Serverless
Kafka applications using IAM, CloudWatch, and KMS integration
notGoodFor: Tiny workloads where broker economics are inefficient
Cross-cloud portability
Teams expecting AWS to design topics, partitions, retention, and consumers
pros: Runs Apache Kafka APIs with AWS-managed broker infrastructure.
VPC networking, IAM auth options, CloudWatch, KMS, and AWS integrations fit cloud-native estates.
Provisioned and serverless choices cover steady and variable workloads.
Reduces broker replacement and infrastructure maintenance work.
cons: Teams still own topic design, partitions, retention, producers, consumers, and many version decisions.
Cross-AZ traffic, storage, broker hours, and connector infrastructure can be costly.
AWS-specific operational model and networking reduce portability.
tools.costEstimate: Usage-based broker or serverless pricing plus storage and transfer; provisioned production clusters commonly start in the hundreds of dollars per month
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.

tools.name: Confluent Cloud
tools.description: Confluent Cloud is a managed Kafka-compatible data-streaming platform with hosted clusters, connectors, schema registry, stream governance, Flink capabilities, and enterprise operations built around the Kafka ecosystem.
bestFor: Managed Kafka with hosted connectors, schema registry, governance, and Flink
Multi-cloud event-streaming programs
Teams reducing broker operations while retaining Kafka APIs
Enterprise CDC and data-product platforms
notGoodFor: Cost-insensitive assumptions about retention and throughput
Teams avoiding managed-platform coupling
Tiny queue workloads
pros: Managed platform removes most broker operations and accelerates production adoption.
Connector catalog and schema services reduce integration work.
Enterprise governance, monitoring, and multi-cloud availability suit large event estates.
Strong Kafka expertise and commercial support are available from Confluent.
cons: Consumption-based pricing can become expensive without capacity and retention discipline.
Confluent-specific managed features increase platform coupling.
Teams still need event contracts, partition strategy, and consumer-operability standards.
tools.costEstimate: Usage-based managed pricing for clusters, throughput, storage, connectors, and networking; entry tiers start low but production bills can reach hundreds or thousands per month
tools.addedReason: Included in the user-supplied registry specification.

tools.name: Aiven for Apache Kafka
tools.description: Aiven for Apache Kafka is a multi-cloud managed Kafka service with automated provisioning, upgrades, security, observability integrations, connectors, and API or Terraform-driven operations.
bestFor: Managed Kafka across multiple cloud providers

Kafka workloads requiring Terraform automation, monitoring, and support

notGoodFor: Lowest-cost hobby streams

pros: Multi-cloud regions help platform teams standardize Kafka operations across providers.

cannotConnectToReason.waf: WAF filters HTTP traffic. Kafka uses binary protocol on port 9092. WAF has nothing to inspect.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating MQTT Broker as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A messaging component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

cannotConnectToReason.mongodb: Application pods may use MongoDB, but the Kubernetes control plane itself must not be modeled as a MongoDB client.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Infrastructure as Code as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A infrastructure component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A infrastructure component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Virtualization Platform as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A infrastructure component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

tools.analogy: Kubernetes is like a port manager for shipping containers — it decides where containers should run, replaces damaged ones, and moves work when a dock becomes unavailable.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating GitOps Controller as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A infrastructure component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A infrastructure component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Cloud Cost Management as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A infrastructure component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Software Supply-Chain Security as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A security component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Cloud Security Posture Management as a single point of failure
commonMistakes.reason: A production component can fail independently or become unavailable during zone and region incidents.
commonMistakes.fix: Deploy redundant instances where applicable, add health checks, and document failover behavior.

commonMistakes.reason: Unbounded traffic, queues, or connections can turn a localized slowdown into a cascading failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Define quotas, timeouts, concurrency limits, saturation alerts, and load-test thresholds.

commonMistakes.reason: A security component without access controls and telemetry becomes difficult to operate and audit.
commonMistakes.fix: Enable least privilege, encryption where relevant, logs, metrics, alerts, and retention policies.
